why: "The LLM knows the design of famous sites by name" is the more natural word order, and nothing else differs.
"If you are stuck" reads more naturally than the clipped "If stuck" and costs no extra words, so A wins.
Drops the extra 'First'; fewer words, same meaning.
'Plausible' is the more precise word for a fabricated answer, and 'blank' is the plainer one; the 'believable' wording in A could read as asking for a convincing fake.
"If in doubt, check before uploading" is shorter and plainer; the difference is a few words, and the shorter wording wins.
"Clues that live apart" is more natural and concrete than "stored apart".
Same content; B opens the bullet lead-in on the action and the file, reads more directly.
Same meaning, A is shorter; 'without any' adds a word for nothing.
'Split' is the plain everyday word and matches the other uses; 'Divide' is stiffer and adds nothing.
'Split an agent doing two jobs' is plain and concrete; 'Divide an agent handling two jobs' is stiffer and wordier.
'A single passing test is one sample' reads more naturally and keeps the same meaning; the difference is tiny.
'Sit on top of normal company controls' is the plain, concrete picture; 'are added to' is vaguer.
'is sitting in the report' is plainer and more concrete than the stiffer 'is found in the report'.
'ends up safe and useless' is the more precise claim, since the outcome is conditional on scoping down far enough; B's flat 'is safe and useless' overclaims.
'Support everything the claim says' is plainer than 'back everything the claim states', and a plain verb fits the author's register.
'Compare it with' is the literal act. 'Check it against' repeats 'check', which the author flags as implying a full read, and the next sentence already uses 'a check'.
"Trained on" names the actual mechanism and reads more plainly than "learn from" followed by "looks like it".
"Returns" matches the sentence on the same point in the lecture slide, which is the plainer verb; "produces" is a bit more abstract.
"Any later run, on any topic, begins from" is plainer and more precise than "The next run... starts"; same length, no added claim.
"Need to be true" is the natural question form and "press send" is the literal act; "hit send" is looser slang.
"A grounded claim can still be vague" is shorter and has a concrete subject, with no loss of meaning.
"That does not work for a system" reads more naturally than "This does not work", and the two are otherwise identical.
Only difference is 'someone has to keep it running' vs 'must'; 'has to' matches the parallel earlier clauses and avoids duty-framing. 'Must' is a stiffer obligation word.
'the part with a name on it' is plainer and shorter than 'that has a name on it'; fewer words, same meaning.
'in Module 6' is a plain locator; 'from Module 6' is slightly odd, and the difference is minor, so B reads cleaner.
'objects; revises' is plainer, more literal verbs than 'pushes back; rewrites', neutral register.
"Without the sponsor" is shorter and plainer; "names the decision provisional" is also tighter than "labels".
"Lives in" is the plainer, more literal verb; "runs in" is slightly odd for a folder.
